title: Control of smallpox in Delhi Municipal Corporation / by P.H. Jeswani

sections.title: Page 1

summary.text: The first page of a 1972 seminar paper on controlling smallpox in the Delhi Municipal Corporation, describing the administrative units of Delhi and the corporation's role in the national eradication programme. It outlines the organisation of the eradication work in the city.

sections.extract: WORLD HEALTH ORGANIZATION SE/WP/72.14 INTER-COUNTRY SEMINAR ON SURVEILLANCE IN SMALLPOX ERADICATION INDEXED New Delhi, 30 October - 2 November 1972 CONTROL OF SMALLPOX IN DELHI MUNICIPAL CORPORATION by Dr P. sections.title: Page 2

summary.text: Describes Delhi's smallpox control staff and structures, including 138 door-to-door vaccinators who also search for fever with rash, and 55 birth, death and vaccination centres that act as reporting points. It notes the use of bifurcated needles and freeze-dried vaccine, giving near-complete success in primary vaccination, though only 60–70% of vaccinations are inspected.

sections.title: Page 3

summary.text: Reports scar surveys from 1970 and 1972 showing over 90% vaccination coverage among children up to 14 years in all eight zones of Delhi. It reviews the trend in smallpox cases and notes that many 1972 cases were imported, some admitted directly to the infectious diseases hospital from neighbouring states, with all eight zones affected.

sections.title: Page 4

summary.text: Lists the 1972 smallpox outbreaks and cases by zone in Delhi, totalling 100 cases in 53 areas, and traces many sources of infection to neighbouring states such as Uttar Pradesh and Haryana. It criticises vague source reporting and stresses the need for proper epidemiological investigation, given the many single-case outbreaks.

sections.title: Page 5

summary.text: Describes a new weekly smallpox reporting system in Delhi, with nil reports required and daily checks with the infectious diseases hospital, and closes with the author's acknowledgements.

sections.extract: SE/WP/72.14 page 5 The recently introduced weekly smallpox epidemic reporting system has been established. Ail the 32 Vaccination Inspectors have been instructed to submit weekly smallpox epidemic reports of their areas regularly, and in time. Even 'NIL' reports are being insisted upon. The Medical Superintendent of the 1.D. Hospital, Delhi, is contacted by telephone daily regarding any admission of a smallpox case.
